transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I just can’t sit still in these meetings or trainings anymore—I feel like I’ve got to get up and move even when everyone else is fine staying put. It's gotten to the point where it's causing some real issues for me at work.
Besides feeling unable to sit still, do you also often make careless mistakes, have trouble focusing or finishing tasks, or lose things because you’re distracted?

To be honest, I don't really have trouble with losing things or getting easily distracted by other stuff. Any mistakes I make, like with our new scheduling system, are more about me rushing through it and being impatient because I'm just itching to get up and move.
Have you had this same restlessness or need to move around since childhood or in more than one setting, like at home as well as at work?

Yes, my mom still talks about how my grade school teachers would call her because I couldn't stay in my seat and kept wandering around. It happens at home too—my wife and kids joke that I'm like a wind-up toy because I can't even sit through church, bingo, or a game on TV without pacing, tapping, or fidgeting.
Before age 12, did these restlessness or hyperactivity symptoms already cause problems for you at school or at home, and have they continued consistently since then?

Yes, they definitely go back to my childhood; my mom still talks about how my grade school teachers called home because I couldn't stay in my seat, kept blurting out answers, and got sent out of class for wandering. While I've always been active and talkative, it never caused this much trouble until my promotion a year and a half ago. Since then, having to sit through those long meetings has made it impossible to manage.
Do your restlessness and difficulty sitting still cause problems in more than one area of life, such as at work, at home, or in social situations, and not just during stressful meetings?

Yes, it definitely affects more than just work. It causes arguments with my wife because I can't sit still through church or bingo nights, and I can't even watch a game on the couch without constantly moving or making noise. On top of that, it's led to me messing up our new scheduling system at work and getting written up.
Did these restlessness and impulsive behaviors continue steadily from childhood into adulthood, or did they start only after your job promotion?

I've actually been this way my entire life, always known as the guy who is constantly on the move. It only became a major problem about a year and a half ago when my promotion forced me into a desk-bound, meeting-heavy role. Before that, my active job let me work around it, but now I'm expected to sit still for hours.

Have you also had frequent impulsive or rule-breaking behaviors since childhood, such as interrupting others, acting without thinking, getting into fights, lying, stealing, or being suspended from school?

I definitely had trouble with interrupting and blurting out answers in school, which got me sent out of the classroom quite a bit. But I never got into fights, lied, or stole—it was just me being unable to keep quiet or stay in my seat.
Do you also have ongoing problems with inattention, such as making careless mistakes, not finishing tasks, or being easily distracted, or is it mainly the restlessness and impulsivity?

It’s definitely the restlessness and impulsivity rather than being easily distracted. The real issue is that I just can't sit still, and my impatience makes me rush through things or jump in too fast before I've even finished listening.

Do you also often act before thinking, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or making impulsive decisions that cause problems? Or is it mainly the restlessness and inability to sit still?

It is definitely both. In staff briefings, I constantly cut people off and blurt out answers before my supervisor even finishes speaking, which often leads to misunderstandings. I also get extremely impatient waiting my turn—whether in meetings, standing in lines, or playing bingo with my wife—and end up jumping in out of turn because I just can't stand the wait.
Have you also had clear problems with impulsivity in daily life, such as interrupting people, blurting out answers, or acting without thinking, or is it mostly just being unable to sit still?

It is definitely not just about sitting still; the impulsivity is a major struggle for me too. In our staff briefings, I frequently cut people off and blurt out answers before my supervisor even finishes his question. I also have a really hard time waiting my turn in lines, meetings, or even playing bingo with my wife, which makes me impatient and causes me to jump in out of turn.
Before age 12, did you also have clear impulsive behavior problems at school or home, like interrupting, blurting out answers, or acting without thinking, or was it mainly being unable to sit still?

It was definitely a mix of both even back then. My mom still talks about how my grade school teachers would call her because I couldn't stay in my seat and would wander around the room. At the same time, I was always blurting out answers instead of waiting my turn to speak.
Do you also have ongoing problems with inattention, like being easily distracted, losing things, or not finishing tasks, or is it mainly hyperactivity and impulsivity?

It's almost entirely the hyperactivity and impulsivity. I don't really have trouble with losing things or being easily distracted. Instead, my biggest issues are this intense physical restlessness where I just can't sit still, my tendency to blurt out answers, and my extreme impatience.

It sounds like your main problems are hyperactivity and impulsivity rather than inattention. Have you ever had a long-term pattern of being easily distracted, losing things, or not finishing tasks because your mind wanders, even outside of stressful situations?

No, I haven't really noticed those kinds of problems with distraction or losing things. My main struggle has always been the physical restlessness, needing to move, and blurting things out. It's the constant urge to be active that gets in my way, rather than my mind wandering.
Did these restlessness and impulsive behaviors clearly start before age 12 and continue in more than one setting, like at home, school, and work?

Yes, they absolutely started before age 12; my mom still talks about how my grade school teachers called her because I couldn't stay in my seat, wandered the classroom, and blurted out answers. It definitely affects me in multiple settings today too, from being unable to sit still on my days off at home to struggling through church and bingo nights with my wife.
Did these symptoms continue without a long break from childhood into adulthood, or were there periods when they mostly went away for years at a time?

They've been continuous since childhood, and I've always been known as a highly active, talkative guy who couldn't sit still. It never really went away, but it only became a major problem recently because my previous jobs allowed me to stay on the move all day. Now, this promotion forces me to sit in meetings and offices, which has made it impossible to manage.
To confirm the timeline, did your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity clearly begin before age 12 and continue steadily into adulthood without long symptom-free periods?

Yes, they definitely go back to my childhood, and my mom still talks about how my grade school teachers constantly called her because I couldn't stay in my seat, kept blurting out answers, and wandered around. I've been highly active and talkative my entire life without any breaks. It only became a major problem recently because my new supervisory role forces me to sit still at a desk and in long meetings.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports a lifelong pattern beginning before age 12 of hyperactivity and impulsivity across multiple settings, with clear functional impairment at work and in social/home situations. He confirms inability to sit still, excessive fidgeting/pacing, blurting out answers, interrupting, impatience, and difficulty waiting his turn. Inattention symptoms are specifically denied or minimal, making ADHD predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation the best fit among the provided candidate codes.
